rounds.proof_sketch: When all inputs are float32, .float() is a no-op. But with negative as float64, original converts to float32 successfully while mutant passes float64 directly to CUDA kernel which throws TORCH_CHECK exception.
rounds.survival_reason: Under standard float32 inputs, the mutation is semantically equivalent because calling .float() on an already-float32 tensor is a no-op. The 112 rounds of testing all used float32 inputs per the default specification, hence bitwise equivalence. The mutation only manifests when the negative tensor arrives with a different dtype, which the original code would convert but the mutant passes through unchanged.
rounds.kill_strategy: Pass the negative tensor with dtype=torch.float64 (or float16). The original code's .float() will convert it to float32, allowing the kernel to execute successfully. The mutant skips conversion, causing the CUDA kernel's dtype check to fail with an exception.
rounds.recommendations: Mutation testing should include dtype variation as part of the test oracle, not just value variation. Explicit type casts in preprocessing code are often defensive guards that only activate with non-standard inputs. Testing coverage should include dtype edge cases even when specifications nominally require specific dtypes.

def generate_inputs(device):
    torch.manual_seed(42)
    anchor = torch.randn(128, 4096, dtype=torch.float32, device=device)
    positive = torch.randn(128, 4096, dtype=torch.float32, device=device)
    # Use float64 for negative - original will convert, mutant will not
    negative = torch.randn(128, 4096, dtype=torch.float64, device=device)
    return [anchor, positive, negative]
